title: Which Safety Benchmarks Have Item-Level Data Suitable for IRT? A Systematic Audit

original_idea.body:
# Which Safety Benchmarks Have Item-Level Data Suitable for IRT? A Systematic Audit

**Problem:** Apply IRT to AI safety benchmarks

**Direction:** Conduct a systematic audit of publicly available AI safety benchmarks (e.g., AdvBench, HarmBench, SALAD-Bench, WildGuard, AIR-2024) to determine which ones release item-level binary or polytomous response data across multiple models, and whether sample sizes (number of model × item cells) meet minimum IRT calibration thresholds (typically N > 200 respondents and > 20 items per dimension).

**Why it matters:** IRT requires item-level response matrices, not just aggregate scores. Before any IRT analysis of safety benchmarks is possible, someone must establish which benchmarks are even analyzable. This is the prerequisite gate for the entire parent problem and is currently undocumented.

**Relevant context:** tinyBenchmarks (2024) successfully applied IRT to Open LLM Leaderboard, MMLU, and HELM because those benchmarks expose item-level data. Safety benchmarks may not. The PSN-IRT framework (2025) ran IRT on 12 LLMs across 11 datasets but did not focus on safety-specific benchmarks. 'Lost in Benchmarks' (2025) similarly worked with general capability benchmarks.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Vague impact. This is a prerequisite audit that catalogs data availability. It does not itself reduce risk; its value is enabling future IRT analyses. The impact chain requires subsequent work to materialize.

low_compute.reasoning: Purely a literature review and data availability audit. No compute needed beyond web browsing.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Checking whether benchmarks release item-level data and counting sample sizes is straightforward documentation work accessible to beginners.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Tightly scoped: audit 5-10 benchmarks for data availability against IRT requirements. A clear checklist-style deliverable that can be completed in a focused effort.

quick_reasoning: Directly addresses a prerequisite for IRT-based safety evaluation with a concrete systematic audit approach; safety relevance is clear as a foundational enabling study.
